title: He wasn’t fighting for Moses’ body.
paragraphs:
He wasn’t fighting for Moses’ body.
He was fighting for ownership.

Because if the enemy would contend over a dead man…
what do you think he’s trying to do with a living one like you?
There’s a scene most people skip.
Epistle of Jude 1:9 tells us that Michael the Archangel disputed with the devil over the body of Moses.

No details.
No full explanation.
Just tension.
And that tension is screaming something deeper.
Some battles don’t look like battles.

They look like thoughts you can’t silence.
Habits you keep hiding.
Memories that whisper, “You’ll never be clean again.”

You smile in public.
But inside?
Because the enemy doesn’t always come with horns.

“You messed up too much.”
“God won’t use you anymore.”
“You’re disqualified.”

“The accuser of the brethren… who accuses them day and night before our God.”
— Book of Revelation 12:10

A man chosen by God.
A leader.
A deliverer.

In Book of Numbers 20:12, Moses disobeys God.
Because of that, he doesn’t enter the Promised Land.
“Look at him. He failed. He disobeyed. He doesn’t deserve honor.”
Because here’s the truth most people avoid:
The enemy’s accusations often contain fragments of reality.
You did hide things no one knows.
And shame builds its case like a prosecutor who never sleeps.
Something happens in Jude 1:9 that changes everything.
He doesn’t defend Moses with logic.
Because the victory was never going to come from argument—
Because whether you realize it or not…
There has been a case built against your life too.

Every sin.
Every secret.
Every moment you knew better but did it anyway.
And if the story ended there—

No hope.
No defense.
No future.
But the Gospel interrupts the courtroom.

“If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.”
— First Epistle of John 2:1
He doesn’t pretend it didn’t happen.
He does something far more powerful—
At the cross, every accusation against you was not ignored.

“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
— Epistle to the Romans 8:1

So when the enemy whispers,
“You’re still that person…”
He’s speaking from a courtroom that has already been closed.
And here’s where it gets even deeper.

“He buried him… but no one knows his burial place to this day.”
— Deuteronomy 34:6

Some scholars interpret that God hid Moses’ body to prevent idolatry.
To stop people from worshiping the man instead of God.
Can become dangerous when they replace God.
In Gospel of Matthew 17, Moses appears again.
Standing with Jesus at the Transfiguration.
The man the enemy could accuse…
Was still restored into God’s presence.
Because your failure is not your final identity.
Your sin is not your final sentence.
Your past is not your permanent name.
Jesus didn’t come to make bad people slightly better.
He came to make dead people alive.
But here’s the question you can’t avoid:
One reminds you of your past.
If there’s sin you’ve been hiding—
If shame has been choking your identity—
Lay it down at the cross.
If you’ve been trying to fight accusations with your own strength—
Because the same God who defended Moses…
